paper.title: Online Bandit Learning against an Adaptive Adversary: from Regret to Policy Regret

settings.name_in_paper: Online bandit learning against an adaptive adversary (unbounded memory), policy regret (lower bound)
unmapped: performance measured by policy regret: loss compared with the loss the learner would have suffered had it played the comparator sequence (adversary reacts to it)
holds for any action set X (construction is generic)
settings.definition_quote: Define the player's policy regret compared to a competitor class C_T as E[sum_t f_t(X_{1..t})] - min_{(y_1..y_T) in C_T} sum_t f_t(y_1,...,y_t).

settings.name_in_paper: k-armed bandit against an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary (policy regret)
unmapped: adversary is m-memory-bounded: loss depends only on the m+1 most recent actions
performance measured by policy regret against constant action sequences
m is not known to the algorithm
settings.definition_quote: An m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary is an adversary that is constrained to choose loss functions that depend only on the m + 1 most recent actions.

settings.name_in_paper: Bandit convex optimization against an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary (policy regret)
unmapped: adversary is m-memory-bounded
policy regret
losses convex in the last argument only (functions of action history)
settings.definition_quote: Let X ⊂ R^d be a closed bounded convex set with diameter D and let F_t be the class of functions from X^t to [0, 1] that are convex and L-Lipschitz in their last argument.

settings.name_in_paper: Bandit linear optimization against an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary (policy regret)
unmapped: adversary is m-memory-bounded
policy regret

settings.definition_quote: Let X ⊂ [−2, 2]^d be a polytope (or, more generally, let X ⊆ R^d be a convex set over which linear optimization can be done efficiently). Let F_t be the class of functions from X^t to [0, 1] that are linear in their last argument.

policy regret
settings.definition_quote: Let X be the power set of {1, . . . , k} and let F_t be the class of functions from X^t to [0, 1] that are submodular in their last argument.

policy regret
settings.definition_quote: Let X be a convex set and let F_t be the class of functions from X^t to [0, 1] that are linear in their last argument.

unmapped: adversary is m-memory-bounded
policy regret against sequences with at most s switches

settings.name_in_paper: Generic online bandit learning against an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary (reduction)
unmapped: arbitrary action set X and loss classes F_t with values in [0,1]
adversary is m-memory-bounded
policy regret (or policy Phi-regret / switching policy regret)
base algorithm A with standard regret bound R(J) against adaptive adversaries
settings.definition_quote: An m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary is an adversary that is constrained to choose loss functions that depend only on the m + 1 most recent actions.

algorithms.name: Mini-batched Abernethy-Hazan-Rakhlin algorithm ignoring first m losses per batch

source.quote: For any player there exists an adaptive adversary such that the player's policy regret compared to the best constant action sequence is Ω(T).

results.notes: Quantity is policy regret (not in vocabulary). Proof gives pT where p=Pr(X_1=y) for some action with positive probability.

symbols.R: monotone standard-regret bound of base algorithm A against adaptive adversaries

conditions: base algorithm A has regret <= R(J) vs constant actions against any adaptive adversary (1-memory-bounded suffices, Sec 4.1)

source.quote: If τ > m, the policy regret of Aτ, compared to the constant action y, is bounded by E[sum_t f_t(X_{1,...,t}) − f_t(y^t)] ≤ τ R(T/τ) + Tm/τ + τ.

results.notes: Policy regret against constant action y.

symbols.C_R: constant C in base regret bound R(J)=C J^q + o(J^q)
symbols.q: exponent of base regret bound, in (0,1)

source.quote: Specifically, if R(J) = CJ^q + o(J^q) for some C > 0 and q ∈ (0, 1), and τ is set to C^{−1/(2−q)} T^{(1−q)/(2−q)}, then E[...] ≤ C' T^{1/(2−q)} + o(T^{1/(2−q)}), where C' = (m + 1)C^{1/(2−q)}.

results.notes: Leading term exact with an additional o(T^{1/(2-q)}) term; recorded as O.

source.quote: The policy regret of the mini-batched version of the EXP3 algorithm (Auer et al., 2002), with batch size τ = (7k log k)^{−1/3} T^{1/3}, against an m-memory bounded adaptive adversary, is upper bounded by (m + 1)(7k log k)^{1/3} T^{2/3} + o(T^{2/3}).

results.notes: Policy regret; leading term exact plus o(T^{2/3}).

conditions: X closed bounded convex set with diameter D
losses convex and L-Lipschitz in last argument, values in [0,1]

source.quote: The policy regret of the mini-batched version of Flaxman, Kalai, and McMahan's algorithm (Flaxman et al., 2005), with batch size τ = (18d(√LD + 1))^{−4/5} T^{1/5}, against an m-memory bounded adaptive adversary is upper bounded by (m + 1) 18d(√LD + 1)T^{4/5} + o(T^{4/5}).

results.notes: PDF extraction lossy about parentheses; per Theorem 2 C'=(m+1)C^{4/5}, so the 4/5 power applies to 18d(sqrt(LD)+1)T.

conditions: X ⊂ [-2,2]^d polytope or convex set with efficient linear optimization

source.quote: The policy regret of the mini-batched version of McMahan and Blum's algorithm (McMahan & Blum, 2004), with batch size τ = (15d)^{−3/4} T^{1/4}, against an m-memory bounded adaptive adversary is upper bounded by (m + 1)(15dT)^{3/4} + o(T^{3/4}).

conditions: losses submodular in last argument over power set of {1..k}

source.quote: The policy regret of the minibatched version of Hazan and Kale's algorithm (Hazan & Kale, 2009), with batch size τ = (12k)^{−3/4} T^{1/4}, against an m-memory bounded adaptive adversary is (m + 1)(12kT)^{3/4} + o(T^{3/4}).

results.notes: K is size of the ground set k.

tuning: tau = m^{2/3}(16 n sqrt(vartheta) log T)^{-2/3} T^{1/3}
first m losses in each mini-batch ignored

source.quote: The policy regret of the minibatched version of Abernethy, Hazan, and Rakhlin's algorithm (Abernethy et al., 2008) where the first m loss values in each mini-batch are ignored, with batch size τ = m^{2/3}(16n√ϑ log T)^{−2/3} T^{1/3}, against an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary, is upper bounded for all T > 8ϑ log T by 2m^{1/3}(16n√ϑT log T)^{2/3} + O(T^{1/3}).

results.notes: Paper's n is the dimension d. Additional O(T^{1/3}) term.

symbols.R: base algorithm's regret bound vs sequences with s switches

conditions: s fixed and independent of T
base algorithm's regret bound R(J) holds vs sequences with s switches

source.quote: Repeat the assumptions of Thm. 2, except that C_T is the set of action sequences with at most s switches (where s is fixed and independent of T) and A's regret bound of R(J) holds compared to action-sequences in C_J. Then, the policy regret of Aτ, compared to action-sequences in C_T, against the loss sequence (f_t), is upper bounded by τR(T/τ) + Tm/τ + (s + 1)τ.

results.notes: Switching policy regret; s mapped to S_T.

conditions: at most s switches in comparator

source.quote: The policy regret of the mini-batched version of the EXP3.S algorithm, with batch size τ = (7ks log(kT))^{−1/3} T^{1/3}, compared to action sequences with at most s switches, against an m-memory bounded adaptive adversary, is upper bounded by (m + 1)(7ks log(kT))^{1/3} T^{2/3} + O(T^{1/3}).

results.notes: PDF extraction lossy on parentheses; additional O(T^{1/3}) term.

symbols.R: base algorithm's Phi-regret bound against adaptive adversaries

conditions: base algorithm has Phi-regret <= R(J) against adaptive adversaries

source.quote: Repeat the assumptions of Thm. 2, except that now let Φ be any set of action transformations and assume that A's Φ-regret against any sequence of J loss functions generated by an adaptive adversary is upper bounded by R(J). Then, the policy Φ-regret of Aτ against (f_t) generated by an m-memory-bounded adaptive adversary is bounded by τR(T/τ) + Tm/τ + τ.

results.notes: Policy Phi-regret (internal/swap regret); proof omitted in paper. Comparator is action transformations, not in vocabulary.
